title: 2 Samuel 19:40–43
context: The king crosses to Gilgal, escorted by all the people of Judah and half the people of Israel, and a bitter quarrel breaks out between the men of Israel and the men of Judah over who has the greater claim to the king. Judah stresses kinship with David, while Israel points to its ten parts in the king and resents being left out. The narrator closes by noting that the words of the men of Judah were fiercer, setting the stage for Sheba’s revolt in the next chapter and foreshadowing the later division of the kingdom (compare 1 Kings 12:16). Readers in both traditions commonly read this passage as shared ground about the dangers of tribal rivalry, wounded pride, and harsh words among God’s people. The verse numbers follow the WEB, one lower than the Hebrew numbering in this chapter.

verses.text: So the king went over to Gilgal, and Chimham went over with him. All the people of Judah brought the king over, and also half the people of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see David crossing to Gilgal with Chimham, escorted by Judah and half of Israel. The return is underway, though not fully united.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the partial escort as foreshadowing division. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as setting up the dispute that follows.

verses.text: Behold, all the men of Israel came to the king, and said to the king, “Why have our brothers the men of Judah stolen you away, and brought the king and his household, over the Jordan, and all David’s men with him?”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the men of Israel complaining that Judah stole the king away. Jealousy surfaces quickly, even in the hour of restoration.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the complaint as revealing wounded pride among the tribes. Both traditions commonly read the verse as a warning about rivalry among God’s people (compare Galatians 5:15).

verses.text: All the men of Judah answered the men of Israel, “Because the king is a close relative to us. Why then are you angry about this matter? Have we eaten at all at the king’s cost? Or has he given us any gift?”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Judah answering that the king is their close relative and they have received no special favor. They defend their actions.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Judah’s reply as reasonable in content but provocative in tone. Readers in both traditions commonly see both sides contributing to the conflict.

verses.text: The men of Israel answered the men of Judah, and said, “We have ten parts in the king, and we have also more claim to David than you. Why then did you despise us, that our advice should not be first had in bringing back our king?” The words of the men of Judah were fiercer than the words of the men of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Israel claiming ten parts in the king and resenting being slighted. The narrator notes that Judah’s words were fiercer.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the fierce words as preparing for Sheba’s revolt (2 Samuel 20:1). Both traditions commonly read the verse as showing how harsh speech fuels division (compare Proverbs 15:18).
